text: 2025 Video Interviews: Former CIA Directors & Officers Warn Trump Does Not Have NATO's or Europe's Back

Former CIA Director John Brennan (Times Radio / Express video interview, Feb 18, 2025 & MSNBC interview, March 7, 2025); Former CIA Director & Defense Secretary Leon Panetta (One Decision video podcast, March 6, 2025); Former CIA Officer Bjorn Beam (Agenda Pública, Dec 2025).

CON: Former CIA officials warned on video in 2025 that Trump does not have NATO's back—freezing intelligence and aid to coerce allies and treating Article 5 as conditional—so Europe cannot abolish Britain and France's 515 sovereign warheads. PRO: If Trump does not have NATO's back, the 100 US B61 bombs in Europe (which require the US President's personal launch codes) are 100% useless bluffs that only paint a Russian target on Europe, while European NATO alone outspends Russia nearly 3-to-1 ($559B vs. $190B) to defend itself conventionally.

In March 2025 video interviews after Washington paused military aid and intelligence sharing with Ukraine, former CIA Director John Brennan called the move “a pressure tactic and extortion,” warning that “this move by Washington has increased anxiety among NATO allies about whether the United States can continue to be trusted,” after stating in February 2025 that Trump “likes to deal with strongmen” like Putin rather than backing NATO allies. Former CIA Director and Defense Secretary Leon Panetta (One Decision video podcast, March 6, 2025) and former CIA Officer Bjorn Beam similarly warned that Europe can no longer assume automatic U.S. protection.
Humanitarian impacts and risks of use of nuclear weapons
International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) Position Paper, August 29, 2020.

PRO: A nuclear detonation in or near a populated area causes decades-long radioactive contamination of water, food, homes, and infrastructure with zero adequate medical or humanitarian response possible; the only guarantee against use is prohibition and elimination.

“The scale of destruction and contamination after a nuclear detonation in or near a populated area could cause profound social and political disruption as it would take several decades to reconstruct infrastructure and regenerate economic activities, trade, communications, health-care facilities and schools. No state or international body could address, in an appropriate manner, the immediate humanitarian emergency nor the long-term consequences of a nuclear weapon detonation in a populated area… Notably, owing to the long-lasting effects of exposure to ionizing radiation, the use or testing of nuclear weapons has, in several parts of the world, left a legacy of serious health and environmental consequences that disproportionally affect women and children.”
Global food insecurity and famine from reduced crop, marine fishery and livestock production due to climate disruption from nuclear war soot injection
Dr. Lili Xia, Prof. Alan Robock, Kim Scherrer, Prof. Owen B. Toon et al. (Rutgers University), Nature Food, Vol. 3, Issue 8, pp. 586–596, August 15, 2022.

PRO: Nuclear war soot and radioactive fallout disrupt water, agriculture, crops, livestock, and household food supplies across Europe and the world—starving over 2 billion people in a regional war and over 5 billion people in a US-Russia nuclear war.

“Atmospheric soot loadings from nuclear weapon detonation would cause disruptions to the Earth's climate, limiting terrestrial and aquatic food production… In quantifying impacts away from target areas, we demonstrate that soot injections larger than 5 Tg would lead to mass food shortages, and livestock and aquatic food production would be unable to compensate for reduced crop output, in almost all countries… We estimate more than 2 billion people could die from nuclear war between India and Pakistan, and more than 5 billion could die from a war between the United States and Russia—underlining the importance of global cooperation in preventing nuclear war.”
